newsitem.title: USA: Broaddus says data show desirable economic slowing.
newsitem.headline: Broaddus says data show desirable economic slowing.

text.p: Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond, on Wednesday said the latest statistics on gross domestic product show a slowing in economic growth that he said was welcome.
"The deceleration we've seen in this morning's numbers is desirable," Broaddus told the Export-Import Club of Richmond.

Earlier Wednesday, the Commerce Department reported that gross domestic product grew at an annual rate of 2.2 percent in the third quarter, a marked slowdown from the rapid pace of 4.7 percent in the second quarter.

In his speech, Broaddus reiterated a number of remarks he made about the economy in a speech Tuesday to the Richmond Association of Business Economists. He said that despite the deceleration in growth, evidence lately has shown the economy operating at a high rate of resource utilization in some key sectors.
"The published statistics and the anecdotal evidence ... suggest that currently the economy is operating at a very high level," he said. "You see this especially in labor markets."

Broaddus said the Fed was getting reports of tight labor markets across the country. He pointed out that although payroll employment fell by 40,000 in September, jobs growth this year has been quite strong. Broaddus also highlighted the 5.2 percent unemployment rate, a level that he said has historically been associated with rising wage costs that can lead to inflation.

Broaddus said that he was skeptical of arguments made by some economists recently that the structure of the economy has changed substantially to the point where the old rules on the relationship between unemployment and inflation no longer apply.
"I am not very confident of that," he said of those theories.
Looking at the current inflation picture, Broaddus said so far it appeared tame.

Still, he said certain special factors such as sluggish demand abroad and capital inflows that have helped boost the value of the dollar have so far helped to restrain inflation. However, he added such restraints are "not necessarily going to persist forever."
